section_summary: This section documents U.S. diplomatic, military-intelligence, and consular reporting on alleged Japanese surveying, mapping, fishing, intelligence, procurement, and propaganda activities in Mexico during 1932 and early 1933. Reports focus particularly on Sonora, Chihuahua, Baja California, and the Gulf of California, but repeatedly distinguish rumor and hearsay from verified evidence. A substantial portion concerns pro-Japanese, anti-American pamphlets and newspaper articles predicting a Japanese-American war and urging Mexico to side with Japan, along with investigations of Japanese fishermen and naval attaché Kohei Ochi.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Adjutant General: Japanese Activities in Mexico
subfiles.from: Alfred T. Smith, Colonel, General Staff, A.C. of S., G-2
subfiles.about: Directs follow-up investigation of reports that Japanese engineers were mapping strategic areas of Chihuahua near the United States border.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum recounts a report of fourteen Japanese engineers using surveying instruments west of Pearson, Chihuahua, and relates it to earlier activity in Sonora and near Sierra Pacheco. It asks the Eighth Corps Area to confirm the reports and watch for further Japanese activity near the border.

subfiles.title: Confidential Mail Instruction No. 540
subfiles.about: Notifies the ambassador of additional War Department communications concerning alleged Japanese activities in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The instruction refers to an earlier State Department communication and states that the War Department sent the military attaché a February 11 communication. Its enclosures reportedly included a Fort Bliss report and a memorandum for the Adjutant General.

subfiles.title: Supplementary Confidential Mail Instruction No. 543
subfiles.about: Corrects the previous instruction concerning what the War Department sent to the embassy's military attaché.
subfiles.summary: The Department explains that the February 11 communication mentioned in Instruction No. 540 was not actually sent to the military attaché. Instead, the War Department forwarded a February 16 letter enclosing a February 2 Fort Bliss report.

subfiles.title: Confidential Mail Instruction No. 549
subfiles.about: Transmits Department of Justice material about alleged Japanese activities in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses a February 19 Department of Justice letter and a special agent's report. Page 75 is the associated file-number backer for record 894.20212/323.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division Distribution Sheet
subfiles.to: Internal military and State Department distribution
subfiles.about: Records internal routing of intelligence material to military branches and State Department divisions.
subfiles.summary: The sheet lists War Department, Army, Naval Intelligence, State Department, and Commerce Department recipients. It appears to be the distribution cover for the following intelligence report.

subfiles.title: Extract Copy of Report No. 3770: Japanese Activities in Mexico
subfiles.from: Robert E. Cummings, Acting Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese arrivals at Pacific ports and discusses a rejected Japanese colonization proposal.
subfiles.summary: A source reported that Japanese groups landed at Guaymas with surveying, photographic, and mapping equipment and that 316 Japanese entered through Pacific ports between October 1931 and January 1932. Major Manuel J. Solís said that Calles and President Ortiz Rubio opposed Japanese colonization and that Mexico had rejected a 1928 proposal to colonize the Pacific coast in return for Japanese-built infrastructure. Solís added that restrictive immigration law favored Mexican settlers on reclaimed land.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 49 from Mexico City
subfiles.about: Seeks instructions concerning Robert Dunn's proposed trip to Sonora to observe Japanese engineering activity.
subfiles.summary: Clark reports that Dunn, a Naval Reserve civilian, was expected to visit Sonora and report observations to Naval Intelligence. Clark warned that Mexican authorities might discover the purpose and become irritated, but noted that notification might secure Mexican assistance. He asks whether to notify the Mexican government or allow Dunn to proceed without notice.

subfiles.title: Incident Involving Japanese Fishing Vessel Kamine and American Cannery Tender Vergana
subfiles.from: William A. Smale, American Consul, Ensenada
subfiles.about: Reports an American vessel's improper demand that a Japanese fishing vessel lower the Japanese flag and fly the American flag.
subfiles.summary: The mate of the Vergana assumed that the Kamine was American because San Diego appeared on its stern and ordered its master to replace the Japanese flag with the American flag. The Japanese master complied, while another Japanese vessel, Kazuyo, was also reportedly flying the American flag. Smale avoided an inquiry that might cause publicity, cautioned the Vergana's master, and suggested that authorities examine the vessels' claimed home ports.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division Distribution Sheet
subfiles.to: Internal military and State Department distribution
subfiles.about: Provides an internal distribution list for intelligence correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The sheet lists military branches, Naval Intelligence, State Department geographic divisions, and Commerce Department offices. It serves as an administrative cover to the following correspondence.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities on the West Coast
subfiles.from: W. H. Simpson, Executive Officer, G-2
subfiles.to: Military Attaché, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Forwards intelligence excerpts and a translated anti-American article from El Noroeste.
subfiles.summary: The letter responds to Cummings's February 9 report and sends excerpts from recent correspondence. It also encloses a February 6 letter from Camp Stephen D. Little with a translation of an El Noroeste article described as Japanese propaganda. Copies were supplied to the State Department and Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Excerpts from Recent Correspondence Received in Military Intelligence Division
subfiles.to: Secretary of War and Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2
subfiles.about: Compiles reports of purported Japanese military personnel, reconnaissance, migration, and fishing activity in Baja California, California, Sinaloa, and Sonora.
subfiles.summary: One source alleged that fifteen Japanese army officers, including engineers, secretly mapped the coast between San Diego and Bahía Magdalena from a camp at El Real de Castillo. Another reported movements of apparently well-to-do Japanese men through San Diego and Ensenada and increased activity among Japanese fishermen. A Fort Bliss informant later stated that the Japanese had apparently evacuated Sinaloa and Sonora.

subfiles.title: Letter Forwarding El Noroeste Article
subfiles.from: Gilbert Procter, Intelligence Officer, Camp Stephen D. Little
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: Forwards a translation of a vitriolic article about war between Japan and the United States.
subfiles.summary: Procter states that Mexican newspapers had published several articles about a possible Japanese-American war. He characterizes the February 2 El Noroeste article as the most vitriolic yet encountered.

subfiles.title: War Between Japan and the United States Is Inevitable
subfiles.from: Attributed to Lt. Gen. Kiokatsu Satō
subfiles.about: Argues that conflict with the United States is inevitable and necessary for Japanese expansion and national survival.
subfiles.summary: The article accuses the United States of obstructing Japanese interests in China, Manchuria, Mongolia, Shandong, and Asia generally while humiliating Japanese immigrants in America. It portrays continental expansion as essential because of Japan's population and economic needs. The author concludes that diplomacy will fail and war with the United States is Japan's inevitable destiny.

subfiles.title: Confidential Mail Instruction No. 552
subfiles.about: Advises the ambassador that the War Department sent the military attaché correspondence and a translated newspaper article.
subfiles.summary: The instruction describes a February 23 War Department letter transmitting intelligence excerpts and a February 6 Camp Stephen D. Little communication. The latter enclosed a translation discussing relations between Japan and the United States.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 51 from Mexico City
subfiles.about: Clarifies Robert Dunn's nonofficial status and authorizes him to travel as an ordinary tourist.
subfiles.summary: After consulting Herschel Johnson, Clark told Dunn that Captain Bagley regarded him as a tourist, not as an operative on a secret naval mission. Dunn said he would merely observe and listen. Clark therefore declined to notify Mexican officials and allowed him to proceed with a warning to be careful.

subfiles.title: Confidential Mail Instruction No. 577
subfiles.about: Transmits another Department of Justice special-agent report about alleged Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses a March 4 Justice Department letter and a February 25 special-agent report. Page 96 is the associated file-number backer for record 894.20212/329.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference to Despatch No. 1279
subfiles.about: Directs readers to another decimal-file location for a despatch concerning Japanese food purchases in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references Despatch No. 1279 from Ambassador Clark. It summarizes the subject as the arrival of Japanese agents seeking foodstuffs for the Japanese Army.

subfiles.title: Purchase of Foodstuffs by Japanese Agents in Mexico
subfiles.about: Forwards newspaper reports that Japanese commercial agents were buying Mexican food for the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: Clark encloses press items reporting Japanese agents at Mazatlán and Guadalajara or elsewhere in Jalisco. They were said to be purchasing large quantities of beans and other provisions for Japan's armed forces.

subfiles.title: They Propose to Procure Foodstuffs to Supply the Forces of Their Country
subfiles.about: Reports plans by Japanese commercial agents to purchase large quantities of Mexican food products for forces fighting in China.
subfiles.summary: The article claims that agents arrived at Mazatlán and other points in Sinaloa and Sonora to contract for shrimp, dried tomatoes, salt fish, chickpeas, and other provisions. It predicts economic benefits for Pacific-coast producers and says the merchandise would be shipped by a Japanese line serving American ports.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to the Attorney General
subfiles.from: James Grafton Rogers, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges a Justice Department neutrality report and notes that a redacted copy was sent to Mexico City.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges the Attorney General's March 9 letter enclosing Special Agent W. M. Bott's February 26 report in the case “Unknown subjects. Neutrality laws.” It states that the report, with Bott's name omitted, was forwarded confidentially to the American ambassador.

subfiles.title: Confidential Mail Instruction No. 579
subfiles.about: Transmits a Justice Department report that also mentions an alleged plot by Mexican generals.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses a March 9 Justice Department letter and a February 26 special-agent report on Japanese activities. It highlights allegations that Mexican generals, some reportedly in the United States, planned to overthrow Mexico's government. Page 104 is the associated file-number backer.

subfiles.title: File Backer 894.20212/332
subfiles.about: Marks the file position for record 894.20212/332.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only the decimal-file number. No substantive text survives in this section.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division Distribution Sheet
subfiles.to: Internal military and State Department distribution
subfiles.about: Lists offices to receive or review intelligence material.
subfiles.summary: The sheet provides the standard distribution list for military, naval, diplomatic, and commercial offices. It precedes an April report on Japanese activity in Sonora.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities on the West Coast of Mexico
subfiles.from: W. H. Wilson, Acting Executive Officer, G-2
subfiles.to: Military Attaché, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese naval captain's ceremonious visit to Mexican troops at Lomas and identifies him tentatively as Kohei Ochi.
subfiles.summary: A Camp Stephen D. Little report states that five Japanese, led by a naval captain, observed drills, filmed troops, took notes, and received official honors from General Juan Felipe Rico at Lomas, Sonora. A later Fort Bliss report identified Japanese naval captain Kohei Ochi as traveling to Mexico City to become naval attaché. G-2 considered Ochi likely to be the visitor but had not confirmed the identification.

subfiles.title: File Backer 894.20212/334
subfiles.about: Marks the file position for record 894.20212/334.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only a decimal-file number and no substantive correspondence.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Summary of Despatch No. 1678
subfiles.about: Summarizes an embassy despatch on Japanese propaganda, Juan Mérigo, and arrested Japanese fishermen.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum outlines Mérigo's pamphlet predicting war and urging Mexico to fight the United States, and repeats an allegation that the Japanese minister paid for its publication. It notes that Kohei Ochi appeared well informed about Mérigo. It also connects the arrest of five Japanese fishermen in Sonora with earlier reports of soundings in the Gulf of California.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1678: Japanese Propaganda and Activities in Mexico
subfiles.about: Forwards documents concerning pro-Japanese propaganda and the arrest of Japanese fishermen in Sonora.
subfiles.summary: Clark encloses a conversation about General Manuel F. Enríquez's plan to counter the propaganda of the Japanese minister and Juan Mérigo. He summarizes Mérigo's pamphlet, which argues that Mexico should join Japan in an inevitable war against the United States. Additional enclosures include a defense of the Japanese monarchy and a military attaché's memorandum about Kohei Ochi and detained fishermen.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Simón Báez
subfiles.about: Records Simón Báez's request for embassy assistance in countering Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Báez said General Manuel F. Enríquez wanted to obtain U.S. material to rebut propaganda by the Japanese minister and Juan Mérigo. He asserted that the Japanese minister had paid Mérigo $10,000 to print and distribute his pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Biographical Data of Ex-Brigadier General Juan Mérigo
subfiles.to: American Embassy and Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes Juan Mérigo's military career, political associations, and later business activities.
subfiles.summary: The biography traces Mérigo's service from Chapultepec through the Madero and Carranza revolutions, his promotion to brigadier general, and his removal from the army after opposing the Plan of Agua Prieta. It recounts an unsuccessful attempt to serve in Morocco and his chicle and banana interests. It also notes an unproven allegation connecting him to the Grey Automobile gang and uncertainty about his current income.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Ambassador on Kohei Ochi and Hamaguchi
subfiles.from: Robert E. Cummings, Acting Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Reports conversations with Kohei Ochi about detained Japanese fishermen, alleged soundings, and Juan Mérigo's pamphlet.
subfiles.summary: Ochi questioned Cummings about Kajiro Hamaguchi and four fishermen arrested in Sonora after accusations that they made soundings in the Gulf of California. Ochi repeated a claim that an American agent had paid for the arrests, which Cummings denied. He also admitted discussing pro-Japanese propaganda with Mérigo but said he refused Mérigo's request for a 2,000-peso publication loan; Cummings suspected Mexican action may have followed Calles's earlier promise to stop improper Japanese activity.

subfiles.title: Report No. 4020 on La Guerra Yankee-Japonesa y la Actitud de México
subfiles.from: Robert E. Cummings, Acting Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Summarizes Juan Mérigo's pamphlet and assesses allegations that Japan funded its publication.
subfiles.summary: The report says Mérigo predicted an inevitable Japanese-American war and claimed that Mexico and numerous Latin American states would support Japan. It repeats Simón Báez's statement that the Japanese minister paid Mérigo $10,000, but Cummings doubts the allegation. He also observes that the pamphlet had little circulation in Mexico City.

subfiles.title: Biographical Data of Ex-Brigadier General Juan Mérigo
subfiles.about: Provides biographical information about pamphlet author Juan Mérigo.
subfiles.summary: This version repeats Mérigo's education, revolutionary service under Madero and Carranza, military promotions, and removal from the army. It also covers his trip to Spain, business ventures in Quintana Roo and Veracruz, the unproven Grey Automobile allegation, and uncertainty about his livelihood in June 1932.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Note on Japanese Activities and the Kumano
subfiles.about: Summarizes intelligence reports and a Guaymas consular despatch about Japanese fishermen, mapping, and the seizure of the Kumano.
subfiles.summary: The note reviews Hamaguchi's arrest, allegations that a Japanese dentist mapped landing fields, and the seizure of the Kumano. It says the Guaymas consul found no real evidence that the crew was charting the Gulf for Japan and notes that charts were readily available. A Mexican general instead linked the investigation to smuggling, while also claiming that Mexico would side with the United States in a war.

subfiles.title: Report No. 4038: Japanese Activities in Mexico
subfiles.from: Robert E. Cummings, Acting Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Reports conversations with Kohei Ochi about Hamaguchi's arrest, Gulf soundings, and Juan Mérigo's propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Ochi said Hamaguchi and four fishermen had been arrested and accused of soundings along Sonora, while Japanese contacts alleged American involvement. Cummings denied that the United States had secret agents in Mexico and believed Ochi was probing American knowledge of Japanese activities. Ochi also described Mérigo's request for publication money, which he claimed to have refused, although Cummings thought he knew more about Mérigo than he admitted.

subfiles.title: Extracts on the Kumano Seizure and Japanese Dentist at Guadalupe y Calvo
subfiles.from: Commanding Officer, 25th Infantry, and First Cavalry Division
subfiles.about: Compiles reports on a seized Japanese fishing craft and a Japanese dentist allegedly mapping landing fields.
subfiles.summary: One excerpt reports that Mexican soldiers seized a Japanese fishing vessel, corrected to Kumano, at Puerto Lobos without explaining why. Another alleges that a Japanese dentist at Guadalupe y Calvo mapped landing fields and nearby territory and recruited Mexican laborers for possible work in Japan and Manchuria. The second account rests on information passed through multiple informants.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities in Mexico: Seizure of the Kumano
subfiles.from: L. B. Clapham, Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Forwards an Associated Press report that Mexican authorities seized the Japanese fishing vessel Kumano.
subfiles.summary: The quoted dispatch says Mexican authorities brought the Kumano from Puerto de Lobos to Guaymas and refused to explain the action. Clapham notes that the vessel and a Captain Kumano had appeared in earlier intelligence reports and forwards the item for possible interest.

subfiles.title: Alleged Activities of Japanese Craft
subfiles.from: A. F. Yepes, American Vice Consul, Guaymas
subfiles.about: Investigates rumors that the detained Kumano No. 5 and its Japanese crew were secretly charting the Gulf of California.
subfiles.summary: Yepes identifies the five crew members and reports that the vessel was detained near the Colorado River under central-government orders. He finds no evidence supporting rumors of naval charting and observes that Gulf charts were commercially available and Japanese residents could already have supplied information. General Mariano Garay said the men were being investigated for smuggling, lacked fishing permits, and could not explain two months of activity, but he considered the espionage rumors unfounded.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Note on San Luis Potosí Propaganda Incident
subfiles.about: Summarizes a consular despatch about pamphlet distribution at a Rotary Club dinner and a related newspaper article.
subfiles.summary: The note says a Japanese Rotary member distributed The Yankee-Japanese War and the Attitude of Mexico at a club meeting. The American consul objected that this violated Rotary's ban on political activity. It also notes a newspaper interview predicting a joint Japanese-Soviet invasion of the United States.

subfiles.title: Anti-American Propaganda in San Luis Potosí Being Spread by Japanese Residents
subfiles.about: Reports Antonio Y. Kurachi's distribution of an anti-American pamphlet at a Rotary Club dinner.
subfiles.summary: Shaw states that Kurachi distributed Mérigo's pamphlet at the August 17 Rotary dinner and that Shaw formally objected under Rotary's constitutional prohibition on political activity. Most club members reportedly agreed that Kurachi's conduct was improper, but the incident quickly reached the press. Shaw also forwards an article predicting a Japanese-Soviet invasion and recalls earlier propaganda attributed to Tokichi Umaba.

subfiles.title: Remarks of Consul George P. Shaw at the Rotary Club Dinner
subfiles.about: Objects in Spanish to the use of the Rotary Club for distributing a pamphlet attacking the United States.
subfiles.summary: Shaw invokes the Rotary constitution's prohibition on political participation. He asks the club to reprimand the member who distributed the pamphlet and instruct him not to repeat the action.

subfiles.title: Incident at the Rotary Supper of Last Night
subfiles.about: Reports the confrontation caused by Antonio Kurachi's distribution of Juan Mérigo's pamphlet.
subfiles.summary: The article says Kurachi distributed copies praising Japan and harshly criticizing the United States at the Hotel Progreso. Consul Shaw objected on patriotic and personal grounds and sought a formal clarification. The newspaper states that it would continue following the matter.

subfiles.title: Incidente en la Cena Rotaria de Anoche
subfiles.about: Spanish original of the report about the Rotary Club pamphlet incident.
subfiles.summary: The article describes Kurachi's distribution of a pro-Japanese, anti-American pamphlet and Shaw's immediate protest. It emphasizes respect for the United States within an international organization and for Shaw personally.

subfiles.title: The Invasion of United States Territory by Oriental Forces Is Imminent
subfiles.about: Claims that Japan and Soviet Russia would soon unite to invade the United States.
subfiles.summary: An unidentified Japanese army officer is quoted predicting the collapse of the Hoover administration and a joint Japanese-Soviet offensive. The article attributes Japan's motives to hatred of the United States and Russia's to nonrecognition. It further claims that domestic discontent and the treatment of veterans would leave the United States militarily weak.

subfiles.title: La Invasión de Territorio Norteamericano por Potencias Orientales es Inminente
subfiles.about: Spanish-language original of the article predicting a Japanese-Soviet invasion of the United States.
subfiles.summary: The clipping reproduces the claims translated on pages 144–145. It predicts resignations within the Hoover administration and portrays American labor and veterans as unwilling to support a coming war.

subfiles.title: Japanese Propaganda in the San Luis Potosí Consular District
subfiles.about: Reviews anonymous propaganda letters and a warning about an alleged Japanese military intelligence officer in San Luis Potosí.
subfiles.summary: Shaw reports a year of quiet Japanese propaganda, including two anonymous English-language letters belittling or taunting the United States. A third letter, received January 30, 1933, alleged that a Japanese intelligence officer had predicted an attack on the Philippines between June and September. Shaw notes circumstantial similarities among the letters and discusses Frank Dickinson's close relationship with Antonio Kurachi; the despatch continues beyond page 150.
